title: One dawn, different lives
hookLine: a wedding house at dawn: one cooks, one calls, one prays. the Rig Veda's dawn wakes each creature to its own way of living
carry: svadharma: the dawn wakes each to their own path
tomorrow: The boy bound to the post
last: "HE IS NOT." AND THE ANSWER: SHRADDHA.

lines: EVERYONE WAKES TO A DIFFERENT JOB.
cards: Five-thirty in the morning on a wedding day. One aunt is already frying puris. An uncle is on the phone about the flowers.
A cousin is asleep with her mehndi drying, and a grandmother stands at the window, palms together. Same house, same gray light coming in, and everyone wakes to a different job.
A Rig Veda poet watched the dawn do exactly that to a whole world. Today: the third voice, Ushas, the dawn.

teach.h: USHAS OPENS THE DOORS OF THE DARK.
teach.b: In the Rig Veda, Ushas is the dawn and a goddess, a young woman in bright clothes who opens the doors of the dark. Book one, hymn one hundred thirteen, watches what she does when she comes.
In paraphrase: one she wakes to power, one to fame, one to greatness, one to go after his own aim. To see their different ways of living, the dawn has woken every creature.
That's the picture: one light, and under it a hundred lives starting up, none of them the same, all woken by the same goddess. The hymn doesn't rank them. It watches each one go.
Hindu tradition has a big word for that idea: svadharma, your own dharma, the path that is yours to walk.
Centuries later, in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well.

In the Gita it first means Arjuna's duty as a warrior; many teachers today read it as each person's own path. Either way, it starts in the morning. That's why so many Hindu homes treat waking as a small rite.
In one common morning verse, you look at your palms before anything else: at the fingertips lives Lakshmi, in the middle Sarasvati, at the root Govinda.
Your own two hands, the first thing you see, the place your own day's work begins.

how: Many Hindus keep the hours around sunrise for prayer, bathing and the morning sandhya; in many homes the day starts with a verse said while looking at the palms, karagre vasate lakshmih, whose wording varies by family.

s: in Rig Veda 1.113, the dawn wakes everyone to the same task
one to power, one to fame, one to greatness, one to his own aim: different lives, one dawn.
in the Gita, Krishna says your own dharma done imperfectly beats another's done well
Gita 3.35: better one's own dharma, even imperfect, than another's well done.
the morning palm verse names Lakshmi, Sarasvati and Govinda
in one common version: Lakshmi at the fingertips, Sarasvati in the middle, Govinda at the root.

games.q: everyone around you is headed for the same career. by the dawn hymn and the Gita, what fits?
o: follow the crowd: same light, same road
find your own dharma, even if you walk it imperfectly
stay in bed until the path is obvious
games.why: the dawn wakes each creature to its own way of living, and Krishna says your own dharma, imperfect, is better than another's done well.

practice: Open your hands and look at your palms, the way the morning verse asks. If you pray, say it, or its meaning: Lakshmi at the fingertips, Sarasvati in the middle, Govinda at the root.
If you don't, just look at your hands and ask: what's mine to do today? Name one thing that belongs to your path, not anyone else's, and let it be enough for this morning.

wordCard.voice: Hymns to Agni, and today, to Ushas: the dawn who wakes every creature to its own way of living. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one's own dharma, from sva, own, and dharma. Krishna uses it in Gita 3.35.

carryVoice: Your line: svadharma, the dawn wakes each to their own path. Look at your hands first. Until tomorrow.
